meta.title: MCP Question Bank — Chapter 1: MCP Fundamentals (multi-select)
meta.revision: v2.1 (curated 2026-09-12, 200 items, verified against the 2026-07-28 specification)

questions.question: Which statements about MCP's origin and governance are accurate? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Membership in MCP's maintainer groups is allocated to member companies
Specification changes go through the SEP process with a sponsoring maintainer
The Linux Foundation assigns each MCP revision a semantic version number
Anthropic announced MCP in November 2024 and published the first revision then
MCP was contributed to the Agentic AI Foundation, announced in December 2025

questions.explanation: MCP was announced by Anthropic in November 2024 and became a founding AAIF project in December 2025; changes flow through SEPs. Revisions are dated, not semantically versioned, and maintainer membership is for individuals, not companies.

questions.question: Which pairings of primitive and controlling party match MCP's model? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Tools are model-controlled: the model selects them, with a human able to deny
Prompts are user-controlled: the user explicitly selects them
Tools are user-controlled: only an explicit user command may trigger one
Resources are application-controlled: the host decides what context to attach
Resources are model-controlled: the model reads whichever URIs it wants

questions.explanation: Model calls tools, app reads resources, user picks prompts. D and E swap the controlling party; nothing stops a host from adding UI controls, but the spec's interaction model is as in A, B and C.

questions.question: Which of these are key principles stated in the specification's security section? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Hosts must not transmit resource data elsewhere without user consent
Users must explicitly consent to all data access and operations
Servers must log every tool invocation to a tamper-evident audit store
Tools are arbitrary code execution and need explicit consent before invocation
All MCP traffic must be encrypted with mutually authenticated TLS

questions.explanation: The three key principles are user consent and control, data privacy, and tool safety. mTLS and audit stores are reasonable engineering practices but are not principles the specification states.

questions.question: Which cardinality statements are true of MCP participants? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: One client communicates with exactly one server
One host can manage many clients
One client can multiplex connections to several servers
One remote server can serve many clients
One server may be attached to at most one host at a time

questions.explanation: Host to clients is one to many, client to server is strictly one to one, and a remote server can serve many clients. D contradicts the one-to-one rule; E is wrong because a remote server commonly serves clients from many hosts.

questions.question: Which of these does MCP deliberately leave to the host or the wider ecosystem? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: How consent is presented to the user in the interface
Aggregating context from several servers into one conversation
Which errors a server returns when required request metadata is missing
Which model runs and how it is prompted
The wire format of messages between client and server

questions.explanation: Model choice, consent UX and context aggregation belong to the host. The wire format (JSON-RPC 2.0 with MCP's constraints) and error semantics such as -32602 for a missing required _meta field are defined by the protocol.

questions.question: Which of these are responsibilities of the HOST application rather than of a server? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Running the model and deciding what enters its context
Executing the work behind a tool call against a backend
Maintaining one client connection per connected server
Declaring which tools, resources and prompts exist
Obtaining user consent before data or tools are used

questions.explanation: The host owns the model, the conversation, consent and the client connections — one per server. Declaring the available primitives and doing the work behind a call are what a server does.

questions.question: Which statements about the 2026-07-28 stateless model are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A server must not treat connection or process identity as a conversation
State that spans requests must be referenced by an explicit identifier the client passes
Every request carries its protocol version and client capabilities in _meta
Servers may cache a client's capabilities from its first request on a connection
Statelessness forbids servers from writing to a database during a tool call

questions.explanation: A, B and C restate the statelessness rules. D is exactly what the spec forbids: servers MUST NOT rely on prior requests on the same connection. E confuses protocol statelessness with application state, which is allowed and referenced by handles.

questions.question: Which statements about clientCapabilities in 2026-07-28 are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: They travel in the _meta of each request, not in a one-time handshake
A server that needs a capability the client did not declare fails with -32021
They list the tools the client intends to call during the session
They describe client-side features such as elicitation support
They are sent once and cached by the server for the life of the connection

questions.explanation: Capabilities are per-request because the protocol is stateless, they describe what the client can do (for example handle an elicitation), and a missing required one produces -32021 MissingRequiredClientCapability with HTTP 400. Nothing is cached per connection, and they never enumerate tools.
